speechtext:
Did the individual states controlling education show any objection to interference by the federal government?
Mr. MacNICO'L: No; on the contrary, they assist. Then, although I must hurry along may I make one or two observations about what I found in connection with the installation of pure water systems. From 1,500 to
2,000	towns and cities have been assisted in obtaining pure water, and the results have been very satisfactory. Any hon. member interested in seeing a magnificent system of water purification would be well repaid if he were to inspect the system in Birmingham, Alabama. Under ordinary circumstances neither the city nor the state alone could have done the work, but with the assistance of the United States government it was done. In the whole of the water purification projects $200,000,000 have been spent.
Then, $350,000,000 have been spent in sewage disposal projects. I made a careful survey of the greatest sewage project in the world, namely that of the city of Chicago, where they have built three immense purification plants and have built a tunnel from 24 to 36 feet in diameter under the city. This tunnel is from six to eight miles long, and is placed 60 feet underground. The project provided a great number of men with work.
As another project, outside many cities and bordering canals and rivers dumps of one kind and another have been cleaned out. The best work I saw was done along the Illinois river. They are beautifying that old sewer-ridden river, and eliminating the dumps along its banks. The dumps are being changed into paries and parkettes, a procedure greatly appreciated by the people.
Next I should like to speak about hospitalization. In the United States about $130,000,000 has been spent in this connection, and about 40.000 beds have been added. Any person would be prepared to do a great deal to help those afflicted with the disease. The finest hospital, for tuberculosis, was at Secaucus, New Jersey, and the next in importance was the naval hospital in Philadelphia.
Business men have arrived at the conclusion that playgrounds are necessary, and people in the United. States may be proud of the playgrounds in that country. The United States is spending $13,000,000 in the promotion of playground siport and in that way are helping to maintain the health of their citizens. The best example of this work was in Kansas City.
Then, hurrying along, may I say that I learned of about 50 slum clearance projects which are being carried on adjacent to 35

cities, and that 25,000 model homes have been erected. By these works they are providing employment and at the same time giving health, education and hospitalization to their people. I shall not take time to mention the great numbers of bridges and tunnels which have been built, but will be content by saying that in 1934 employment was provided for 700,000 men at one time. When we consider the great numbers who are behind those men, doing the work in factories, we may add at least another 500,000 to 700,000 more. That is handling relief in a big way, and I would, urge upon the minister that he begin, as soon as he can, to do it, because he is sitting on a volcano, he is in the path of a cyclone, he is facing a great disaster, unless the Canadian people can be put to work. They are not being put to work by the measures offered: by the present government, as was admitted when the minister spoke. A paltry few thousand of the 400,000 unemployed have found work. A considerable number have been taken on in steel plants, in the gold fields and in the nickel business, industries which are dependent on the present war scare in Europe.
May I touch upon one of the great projects which has been undertaken, namely that in the Tennessee valley. I made careful inquiry there, and in view of the recent floods in the Ohio valley, which caused damage to the extent of $500,000,000, I am glad I made the inquiries. If $500,000,000 had been spent to save the Ohio valley as has been spent in the Tennessee valley, much would have .been added to the national wealth, and that $500,000,000 would not have been lost to the country. In the Tennessee valley there are seven large dams-Norris, Gumtersville, Wheeler, Wilson, Pickwick, Chickamiaga and Fowler-ranging in height from 72 feet to 300 feet and in length from 1,265 feet to 7,715 feet. The horse-power production ranges from a low of 66,000 to 261,000. The immense reservoirs give absolute control of the flow of water. During the recent catastrophe extending over the states of Kentucky, Tennessee, Ohio, Indiana and southern Illinois, they demonstrated this absolute control.
I should like to refer to what the minister can do in the province of Ontario as a start, and then carry it on into, the other provinces. Almost daily in the press we read news of floods. Here are some of the headlines :
Fifth flood this winter halts Fergus business.
Waterloo county hit and some residents forced from home.
Port Hope facing acute situation from flood waters. Grand river rises.

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
The towns of Hanover, Kitchener, Galt, Walkerton and many other places are in constant danger from floods. The business section of Port Hope was nearly wiped out last spring; it faced another flood this winter, and there are possibilities that it may be repeated this coming spring.
We read that the Grand river submerges roads adjacent to Galt and causes considerable destruction to adjoining farms.
In order to get a clear insight into this matter of flood control I visited the one place where they are proposing what I consider a perfect flood control plan. I refer to the state of Wisconsin. In that state is lake Winnebago, into which flow the Fox and Wolf rivers, as well as many other smaller streams. The Fox river then continues into Green bay. There are some very important municipalities in this district, such as Fond du Lac, Oshkosh and Menasha. I gave particular attention to the proposed flood control work in the vicinity of Fond d.u Lac, because it approximates the conditions here in Ontario. I obtained some figures from the engineers. The area to be served is 210 square miles. Bad floods occurred in 1905, 1912, 1915 and 1924. The 1924 flood cost the city $700,000. The amount of rainfall at that time was suffi-sient to cover the whole area 2-75 inches deep. The flow of water amounted to 1,342,000.000 cubic feet, which was sufficient to cover the 6-7 square mile area of Fond du Lac to a depth of seven feet. That is just about the depth to which it was covered at the last flood. The rainfall was equivalent to a flow of thirty cubic feet per second' per square mile. The total cost of erecting the five dams necessary to provide this control and prevent a recurrence of these floods is $300,000. Five hundred and seventy men would be employed for four months.
I endeavoured	to	make a	comparisonbetween what had been estimated at Fond du Lac and what should be done at four or five centres in Ontario. The government engineers in Wisconsin told me that these floods are bound to recur with greater frequency and greater volume because of the deforestation of	the	countryside.	Unlessmeasures are taken to prevent them, there will be considerable damage to the cities and the surrounding	countryside.	The	Moira
river flows through Belleville. Its watershed is 1,038 square miles. Applying the Fond du Lac basis of figuring to this river, we find that the flood volume of flow would be 6,650,000,000 cubic feet. During the last flood damage to a total of $300,000 was incurred in the city of Belleville. It would cost $1,500,000 to build the necessary storage dams, which would provide work for four months for 2.800 men.
Coming to the Ganaraska river, which flows through Port Hope, we find that the area concerned is 90 square miles. The volume of flood water would amount to 575,000,000 cubic feet. It would cost $130,000 to provide the necessary works, which would give employment to 250 men for four months. When one looks at the little bridge on the main street of Port Hope and observes that this tremendous flow of water must pass under it, he will realize what is bound to happen. Most of the business houses on the main street of Port Hope south of the St. Lawrence hotel were flooded' out. This is the type of work which should be carried on. It provides a maximum of employment and is much better than the pork-barrel stuff. Many small public buildings are being erected, but this type of work is governed largely by patronage.
I come next to the Grand river, flowing through Galt. The area of the watershed north of Galt is 1,360 square miles, and the flood volume of water 8,700,000,000 cubic feet. The cost of the necessary works would be $2,000,000, and employment would1 be provided1 for four months for 3,700 men. The Thames at London serves an area of 1,100 square miles. The flood flow would be seven billion cubic feet and the cost of the necessary works would be $1,600,000 to provide work for four months for 3,000 men. The Saugeen river at Port Elgin has a watershed of 1,565 square miles. The flood flow here is ten billion cubic feet. The cost of the necessary works would be $2,250,000 but employment would be provided for 4,000 men for four months.
Works of this kind would add millions to the national wealth of this country. I can see the minister presenting a proposition to the city of Belleville whereby this government would agree to advance $1,500,000 for the erection of necessary control works, the money to be returned on a thirty-year basis and paying such low rates of interest as the government could obtain. What a boon such a proposition would be to Belleville. They would know they would be saved from further disaster, and employment would be given to 2.800 of their unemployed for four months. These things are being done in the United States; why should we not do them?
I am sure the minister has the best of intentions but perhaps he has not sufficient background to permit him to grasp matters of this kind. I have no doubt that in time he will gather sufficient information and equip himself to accomplish these things, but I suggest to him that these are matters for engineers and business men. The minister should surround himself with a few township reeves

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
and county engineers and men of that calibre, instead of those who know little or nothing about giving employment to unemployed men. I feel that the government is faced with a golden opportunity. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said last year, the time has come when the government must provide the money with which to go on with the necessary work. Millions would be added to the national wealth by what would be saved through the avoidance of disasters, and in the meantime perhaps a hundred thousand Canadians could be put to work.
I will conclude with this thought. If Canada to-morrow had to enter a war-which God forbid; I am one who believes that he who wants war should be the first to be put in the front line, so that he may get all that is coming to him before the real, honest, wholesouled men who are gathered from all over the country have to go-this government would quickly find a hundred million dollars; it would find five hundred million dollars if it had to. Let the minister put into action those fine principles which he has long taught to classes in the old university at Kingston. He has the opportunity; let him take hold of it and provide employment for the hundreds of thousands who are out of work in this country-I believe the minister admitted that they number around 400,000. There is nothing surer than that if something is not done for these men they will make their voices heard in no uncertain way, perhaps sooner than the government anticipates.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like for a short time to address the house on the amendment. I realize that in this discussion a good deal of latitude has been allowed, but I intend to stick as rigidly as I can to the text. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) moved:
That all the words after the word "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets that the government has failed to take effective measures to deal with the problem of unemployment."
Most hon. members who have spoken have dealt with the budget rather than with the amendment. It is true that some hon. members opposite have made some reference to the amendment and have offered certain suggestions, but I think I am safe in saying that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) who has just sat down has contributed more in the way of suggestions touching the amendment than any other speaker of his party.

When at the end of the leader of the opposition's speech of three hours I heard
the amendment moved, I was astonished, but I assumed that he felt there was nothing else he wished to amend except unemployment, because the government had done so well with all the other measures brought down in the budget. The amendment moved by the leader of the opposition appears to have been an afterthought, because I found on looking up Hansard that his speech covered forty-nine pages, or about ninety-eight columns, and that only five pages or at most eight and three quarter columns were devoted to the subject of the amendment. Of those five pages, the first column was occupied with a recital of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said in 1935; one column gave figures of unemployment during and after 1931; five and a half columns were devoted to the names and salaries of employees of the National Employment Commission, and the remaining one and a half columns were devoted to the merits of his case. When the right hon. gentleman sat down, just on the stroke of six o'clock, I was astounded at the figures as presented by him. I thought that here was an instance where bureaucracy had gone mad, that this commission had engaged such a tremendous number of employees that I expected the newspapers next day to carry headlines something like this: "Tremendous reduction in unemployment in Canada owing to the vast number of employees taken on by the National Employment Commission." It was rather a shock to me, and I wondered what the truth of the matter might be. When, during the evening, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) gave some particulars with regard to the employment of these persons, it seemed to me remarkable that the leader of the opposition, a distinguished lawyer, accustomed to the analyzing of evidence, should go so far astray as to impute to the National Employment Commission responsibility for engaging all the employees that he named. If the Minister of Labour had done nothing more than make that explanation he would, I think, have demonstrated the futility of the amendment.
I do not like to use the tu quoque argument and to say, because we are accused of a certain thing, " you yourselves did the same thing," but the leader of the opposition invited that retort, because he said that he followed the example of the opposition of the day when he was leader of the government, when the opposition moved an amendment similar in form to the one he has now moved.

The Budget-Mr. Glen
I heard my genial friend the hon. member for Davenport speaking this afternoon of " extravagant futility " as being merely academic words, words used only by a college professor, but I would ask him, for he as well as any man knows the value of words, was there ever any more extravagant futility than the efforts made by the government of which he was a supporter from 1930 to 1935? When he takes this critical position with regard to all these projects, one wonders if the lessons of years have not even yet penetrated the Tory mind. For five years, animated by intentions the credit for which we are always ready to give them, the Tory government spent money for the relief of unemployment but missed entirely the essentials of the problem. To-day we find the same kind of arguments being used by the Tory protectionists, that only by providing public works and creating work through employment upon public undertakings can a solution be found. They have absolutely missed the essence of unemployment. It is extraordinary that the hon. member for Davenport should admit, as he did today, that unemployment is not a passing phase. Some of us would like to believe that it is, but a great many of us believe that the effects of unemployment can be considerably minimized by a proper direction of legislative policy.
The hon. member also spoke of the large sums expended in the United States, but it is conceded that they are not thereby curing unemployment. The last figures I saw showed that about 11,000,000 of their people were out of work. Will the hon. member assert that the president believes his administration is abolishing unemployment by these methods? Although great amounts have been spent, there is no apparent diminution in the numbers of unemployed.
Our Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) says frankly that the results of the efforts of the employment commission are not at this moment entirely satisfactory. No one is satisfied. But I think he has the right to take the position that this is not a mere passing phase; it is something that must necessarily involve a long period of education. I would recall to the house that during the five years the leader of the opposition was in power his government were asked to form a commission to deal with the question of unemployment, and it was stated at that time that such a commission would be appointed as soon as the Liberals regained power. They have done what they promised to do, and we are now invited to pass judgment upon what they have done.
There is no one in this house who is not willing and anxious to give the very best that is in him to cure the disease of the body economic to-day. I know that every member, whatever his party, is anxious to find a solution of it; but I wish to point out, and particularly to the members of the Conservative party, that the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite are bound to create unemployment. To-day in the old land there is a good, deal of employment. But how is it created? By something which I hope is only temporary, namely, the building up of armaments. In Germany to-day there is very little unemployment, and for the same reason, the building up of armaments; and in the United States there is also a large measure of employment created by the same agency. I am submitting that the results of that policy, as exemplified in Canada, are such that we have to address ourselves to solving the problem, and I say further that no commission dealing only with the question of unemployment can possibly solve iit unless they go further and deal with the causes of it.
I happened to notice in the Family Herald and Weekly Star of March 3, 1937, the comparative income taxes paid in Canada. The agrarians, representing 31-7 per cent of the population, paid in income tax $56,427; the merchants, $4,354,099; the manufacturers, $15,192,403; the financial people, $10,718,946. Here we see that the agrarians, 31-7 per cent of the population, pay $56,000 odd while the financial men pay $10,718,946. That is a disparity that is prevalent throughout the prairie part of the country, and I believe that to a large extent it is prevalent also in the maritimes. When the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) speaks of the integrity of Canada he must realize, as every one of us does, that if any member of the body is maimed the health of the whole body is impaired to that extent, and with conditions as they are in the maritimes and in the prairies, what is the reason for the present situation in this growing period of prosperity which is indicated in the budget speech? I say you cannot and will not cure unemployment simply by building public undertakings; that is only a palliative which mu^t pass. You have to go further, and when this National Employment Commission is	functioningand it should have the right to function for some considerable time-it should deal with the disparities that prevail in the far eastern parts of the maritimes and in the
The Budget-Mr. Glen

middle west part of the prairies, which as we see it are not getting their share of the prosperity of Canada.
When the leader of the opposition was discussing the question, of unemployment, I thought it would be interesting to find out what results might have accrued from service performed by the employment commission in relation to the strikes that have taken place in Canada in, the last few years, including the time since this government have been in office. I got some figures from the Department of Labour showing the number of strikes and lockouts involving disorders, that have occurred from 1930 to 1936. Those in which riots or arrests and prosecutions occurred were reported; minor disturbances, with pickets and so on, were not included. I find that in 1930 there were five strikes and lockouts; in 1931, fifteen; in 1932, nineteen; in 1933, twenty-three; in 1934, thirty-eight; in 1935 the number began to decrease, there being only eighteen; and in 1936 there were thirteen.
I submit that if the commission has done nothing else to justify its existence, the figures I have quoted show that there has been less disorder in Canada since the Liberals took office and since this national commission has begun to operate; and I suggest that instead of doing that commission the disservice which the leader of the opposition did in his budget speech, we should all cooperate and give it every assistance. The commission should be given the confidence of parliament to go forward in a work which everyone is satisfied cannot be done in a day or a year. But apparently there is to be no cooperation from the leader of the opposition. I submit further that we have to dig and delve much deeper than the commission's functions at present allow.
The leader of the opposition said that one way of getting money was to soak the rich. I do not believe that any of us in this house is anxious to soak the rich, but some of us are really anxious to relieve the poor, and in this regard I would give a warning to the house. We in the west are sometimes met with cries of dissension and secession. Well, Abraham Lincoln once said that the union could not live half slave and half free, and I will go so far as to say that you cannot maintain this nation if you speak of it in terms of east and west. The unity of Canada depends upon that unity among us that is necessary for the survival of all. Those of us in the west who do know the circumstances believe that the agriculturists have not received their share of the plums that are given out in Canada, and when we hear the leader of the 
opposition making the protectionist argument again and referring to the woollen mills that may be affected by the budget, I must say that for my part it leaves me absolutely cold, because I realize that there are men in the west who are not only willing but are working and receive no pay. Moreover, I know that for a number of years past these industries have been receiving much more than they are entitled to in the way of protection. When they speak of the lack of employment, I answer that there is no unemployment on the farms of the west, nor I assume, is there any in the fisheries of the maritimes. Unfortunately, however, their returns do not make the work of these people worth while.
My plea to-day is this-and I will deal with the point further when we come to the main motion that in the endeavour to preserve the unity of Canada there must be some degree of regard for all parties. Surely the time has come, after the experience of high protectionist doctrines in the years from 1930 to 1935, when Canada should begin to try the effect of a policy of lower tariffs, and I believe that the Liberal party, following the present trend noticeable in the budgets of last year and this, is moving along lines that we in the west can support. We would like to hurry them along faster, but nevertheless we are satisfied that their direction is right. Only by dealing with the fundamentals of the economics of this country can unemployment be cured. There is only one way to cure unemployment, and that is by increasing work, and the only way you can increase work is by developing trade between nations.
I submit that the amendment proposed has no bearing on the budget speech. It was indeed a work of supererogation, and despite what was said by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) that every man in this house could support it, I am satisfied that the large majority realize that the amendment is offered as a slight embarrassment to the government and was not intended as seriously as it was offered. For the reasons I have given I intend to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to give a few of what I consider the most important reasons why I am going to support the government and vote against the amendment. I believe the return

The Budget-Mr. Winkler
of prosperity to this country has resulted in large measure from our trade relations with other countries, and further I believe the government has concluded with our best customer, Great Britain, a trade treaty that will facilitate the flow of trade in both directions. I consider it most important that trade should flow in both directions. It is conceded that if we are to sell abroad we must buy abroad, though this may not apply in all particulars to all commodities. In the case of nickel, for instance, we know that nowadays there is such a demand for that commodity that nations will take it at whatever price they have to pay, but with regard to raw materials generally we know that this dominion, producing such commodities in large amounts, must sell them in world markets, and the trade treaty that has been negotiated with Great Britain will increase our ability to sell abroad. As I have said, in return for selling we must buy and, as the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) pointed out this is perhaps one of the most important reasons for supporting the government at this time.
Rather than deal with the whole range of raw materials, the products of the forest, the sea, the mine and the farm, I shall content myself with discussing the products of the farm and in particular our most important commodity in the world market to-day, wheat.

In my constituency a new industry has grown up as the result of the ingenuity of a young mechanic. Most agricultural implement companies manufacture what is commonly known as a grain crusher or grinder. By a very simple invention the young man in question is able to produce in a rural community, where power costs are high but where overhead and labour are comparatively low, an article that he is able to put on the market to compete with implements of a similar kind produced by some of the large implement companies. Railway Act Amendment

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. OSCAR L. BOULANGER (Belle-chasse) moved the second reading of Bill No. 20, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: I do not think it is necessary for me to take up much of the time of the house in explaining this bill. The bill itself is very simple. It proposes to amend one section of the Railway Act to provide that claims against the railways for damages caused by snow fences shall be taken before the board of railway commissioners instead of going through the ordinary courts. Section 20S of the act reads:
Every railway company may, on and after the first day of November, in each year, enter into and upon any lands of His Majesty or of any person lying along the route or line of the railway, and erect and maintain snow fences thereon, subject to the payment of such land damages, if any actually suffered, as are thereafter established, in the manner provided by law with respect to such railway.
2. Every snow fence so erected shall be removed on or before the first day of April then next following.
Up to the present time all disputes between the railway companies and individuals with respect to damages caused by snow fences have had to be taken before the ordinary courts. This generally involves considerable expense and delay, and it was thought better to have these cases come before the board of railway commissioners. There are no costs before this board, while the costs in the courts are sometimes quite heavy. Furthermore, cases brought before the railway board are generally decided more speedily. The board of railway commissioners might be termed a poor man's court, whereas the ordinary courts are sometimes luxuries which the ordinary farmer, especially in these years of depression, cannot afford.
Very often the claims agent of a railway company scares a farmer by mentioning the possible costs involved in an action. The claims agent may suggest a sum to a farmer in settlement and then intimate that if it is not accepted the farmer may sue; but the railway will take the case to the court of appeals, then to the supreme court and even to the privy council in England.
You would have to get a fiat; you cannot sue the crown without a fiat.

I think you can sue the Canadian National Railways, and certainly you can sue the Canadian Pacific

Railway 'Company without first obtaining a fiat from the governor in council. In most cases the amount involved is not large enough to warrant going to the court of appeal, but the farmer may not know this. Quite often the farmer is scared at the possible costs if he takes his claim to court, and for this reason he sometimes settles for almost nothing. I d'o not blame the claims agents of the railways for doing this. Their business is to settle claims for as little as possible, but at the same time I feel the farmer should be given a chance.
At the present time most farmers have no money to go to court. Going to court is a very expensive business, especially in my province. I think it would be doing a great service for the farmers of this country if these cases were adjudicated by the board of railway commissioners instead of being sent through the ordinary channels of court litigation.
It would be quite easy for the railway board to decide these cases as there is very seldom any question of law involved. Speaking for the only province in which I have practised law, I can say that in Quebec the courts cannot award damages which have not yet been incurred. In other words, the courts can award only damages which have actually been incurred. They cannot award a farmer future damages from snow fences; he must wait until they have actually occurred. This means that the farmer must sue at least every two years as damage actions are barred after two years in the province of Quebec. It would be possible for the board of railway commissioners to fix annual damages in connection with the erection of snow fences, and thus obviate the necessity of going to court at frequent intervals.
The damages suffered by farmers located alongside railway lines have increased in recent years. In past years the railways employed ploughs and a different type of snow fence from that in use to-day. The old fence used to be a big, clumsy sawhorse affair which was erected in November, and which was soon covered with snow. It was only about seven or eight feet high and there was not a great deal of snow accumulated against the fence. But a different type of fence has come into use during the past few years. Posts from twelve to fifteen feet high are placed in the ground in the fall. Along these posts is strung a fence of slats, held together by wires. As soon as these slats are covered with snow they are pulled up on the posts to the top of the

Railway Act Amendment
snow, and this process is repeated until the snow has reached the top of the posts. This means that more snow is accumulated and greater damage is done.
I do not think it is necessary for me to give details how this damage occurs. Accumulations of fifteen or twenty feet of snow are not unusual in my section of the country, and this means that the farmer cannot use his land in the spring. This is especially true in my own parish where the railway lines run through many vegetable gardens, strawberry patches and potato fields. These are rendered almost unusable by the accumulation of snow. That snow takes a long time to melt. Sometimes at the beginning of June there is still snow on the ground where these accumulations have gathered during the winter. That prevents the farmer from using some of the most valuable land on his farm for the cultivation of vegetables or strawberries or potatoes. Every farmer knows, of course, that these things have to be planted early in the spring, and at the latest, by the middle of May. If the ground is covered with snow and ice, or with cold water, or if it is soggy, it cannot be used; and if it is not culti-vatable until June the farmer loses almost half of his crop. Potatoes planted in June do not produce as large a revenue as when they are planted in due season; everyone knows that.
For these reasons, for the purpose of providing a quick and inexpensive way of settling farmers' claims against railways due to the use of snow fences, I have presented this bill to amend the Railway Act, and I submit it to the kind consideration of the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I point out that the amending of the Railway Act is considered quite a serious matter. At the present time I have, I believe, some thirty submissions by railway organizations, each of them calling for an amendment to this act. I have pointed out to those organizations that, while some of the amendments they propose are non-contentious, they must await a general revision of the act. I believe that the last amendment was undertaken in 1917 and finished in 1919-nearly twenty years ago-and I think the act is due shortly for further revision.
There is another side to this particular bill, and that is that it changes the nature of the duties of the board of railway commissioners. Under the Railway Act provision is made for settlement by a method of arbitration for claims in respect of snow fences; that is. if the parties cannot agree, the local judge is brought
in as arbitrator. One appeal is allowed, namely to the judge of the superior court, unless the claim is for more than $5,000. In my opinion that is a fairly simple procedure.
This bill proposes a reference to the board of railway commissioners instead of to the local judge. This would mean, I assume, either that the litigants would have to travel to Ottawa to appear before the board, or a section of the board would have to travel to the locality to hear the case. It hardly seems to me that this would be cheaper than to resort to arbitration. A note from the chairman of the board of railway commissioners states that the board has always resisted any attempt to make it a court for the settlement of claims. He points out that the board is not constituted for work of that kind. He also mentions that in 1917, when the act was last revised, an attempt was made to impose upon it duties of this kind, and that the board resisted strongly and successfully having such work assigned to it.
I regret to have to oppose this bill. It could be sent to committee for further discussion, but as I should have to oppose it there, I think the proper time for me to voice my opposition is at the moment, and I therefore ask the house to reject this bill.

I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Boulanger) who has been looking after fences in the province of Quebec. I listened also to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), and in my opinion his answer is not satisfactory. The board of railway commissioners may not be what all of us may think they should be, but nevertheless they are in office. It may be argued that to assign them somewhat trivial duties would not be advisable, and it is clear that this does not appeal to the Minister of Transport. There are many difficulties in reference to the railway situation in Canada. In the past some measure of fairness was meted out to the various provinces, but that principle seems to have gone into oblivion; it has receded into the dark ages. We in the maritime provinces. and particularly in the province from which I come, felt when we signed the pact of confederation that we were doing something against our will. Perhaps I should speak only for myself; other members from the maritimes are here and can speak for themselves. I am neither a leader nor a follower; I am one who loves to live and learn. I say to the Minister of Transport that, in my thought, his answer to the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) was not satisfactory, and this bill should be adopted. I
Government Railways Act

regret very much that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not here on this
occasion.
When it comes to a question of damages, with all the intricacies involved in pursuing a claim, where is the farmer at? He is out in the cold icy snow of which the hon. member has just spoken. Is it to be supposed that the railway commission will be a saviour of all souls, bringing to this young Canada of ours the ideal of universal justice? I do not think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) believes that. I see him there, his brow contracted., his hand over his face.
Why pick on me?

I believe he is sunk, not in iniquity, but in meditation on ideals which will make Canada a great nation.
I hope that the Minister of Transport will not impress his own views on all those around him, because if he does he will be in a whirlpool deep enough to drown him and them. What I have said comes from my heart. I love the right. Perhaps I should not be on this side of the house because I oppose the minister. I recall very well an hon. gentleman who sat on this side in 1923 and who crossed the floor and took the seat which the hon. leader of the reconstruction party occupies to-day. It was -said that the exprime minister was dogmatic, that he was a dictator. In some respects I do not agree with that. At any rate, I say to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) that if he is going to bring anything into this house and try to push it through he will make an awful mistake, because it cannot be done.

As seconder of the motion, I do not think I need add much to what has already been said with regard to this bill. There are one or two arguments I should like to make but at the moment I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

Mr. OSCAR L. BOULANGER (Belle-chasse) moved the second reading of Bill No. 21, to amend the Government Railways Act.
He said: I considered it necessary to amend not only the general Railway Act but also the Government Railways Act, because in the section of country from which I come, which is traversed by the old Intercolonial Railway, formerly owned by the government, we are not quite sure whether the dominion Railway Act or the Government Railways Act applies.

There is still some doubt in the minds of men better trained in the law than I am and for that reason I have proposed the amendment not only of the Railway Act but also of the Government Railways Act so as to cover the ground completely, leaving no loopholes. I am interested in having claims against the old Intercolonial Railway settled to the advantage of my constituents. I hope, if it is not hoping too much, that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) will change his attitude. What I am asking is very little; it would add hardly anything to the duties of the board of railway commissioners, and would do the farmers a great deal of good. We have always claimed that our party stands for the poor people.
Not now.

I am trying to give the government a chance to prove this by fighting the fight of the poor farmer against the big railway companies. The board of railway commissioners travels throughout the country at the present time, and these amendments would not necessitate their travelling any more. There is therefore no argument from that standpoint. They have to travel all over Canada to hear cases that come within their jurisdiction, and if we gave them jurisdiction to try these small damage actions it would not oblige them to do any more travelling nor would it give them any more work to do than they are doing to-day, while it would help the farmers and give them a chance to have claims settled against the railways in an equitable and inexpensive way. In spite of what the minister has said, I submit that these bills will serve a good purpose and should be passed.
On motion of Mr. McLean (Melfort) the debate was adjourned.

trust that the other members of this house who have spoken in this debate in support of the government will not consider me invidious if I select for some attention, two of

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
the speeches delivered, one, that of the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) and the other, that of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). The speech of the former was indeed entertaining and euphonious, and that of the latter a beautiful example of sophistry, yet naive. The hon. member for Huron North started off by telling us that he was a great reader of fiction, particularly of detective stories. I had always suspected that, sir, because in every campaign when I came across that consumer pamphlet of the Liberal party, of which the hon. gentleman is alleged to be the putative father, I thought he must have dwelt in the realm of fiction.
After listening to the Minister of Labour I came to the conclusion that he had probably been infected by the hon. member for Huron North and had also become a great reader of fiction. I shall return to the minister in a moment, however. The member for Huron North, referring to the speech of the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bennett) and his amendment said of him:
He did not perish unless a return to this house, surrounded by a rather diminished band of sometimes mute and somewhat inglorious Miltons, constitutes the act of perishing.
I admit that on many occasions those of us who sit in the Conservative group are mute; it gives us some time for thought; and as we do not have to stand in the glaring light of a self-appointed protector of the consumers of this country we have some little time for reflection. And our time for thought and reflection has thoroughly satisfied us that, at least so far as we are concerned, we cannot accept the proposal of the hon. gentleman from Huron North as a solution of the unemployment problem. In a word or two the hon. gentleman says that what we need in order to solve the problem is a reduction in the cost of manufactured or industrial commodities, and he goes on to propose that industry should be moved out to the small towns in order that cheaper production may be attained. Well, for many years prior to
1932	it has been contended by free traders that the secret of prosperity was low commodity prices. But from my reading, and as a result of our experiences in the depression years 1930 to 1932 or 1933, I think that by
1933 most of the economists even were in agreement that lo- prices were not a solution of the problem; that in fact what was needed was higher prices and not lower prices. Possibly, however, the Minister of Labour might desire to relegate the economists to the realm of fiction.
The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) told of having propounded' a question to a shoe merchant in a town in his riding, which the poor unfortunate shoe merchant, apparently being one of those mute and somewhat inglorious Miltons, was not able to answer. But we are not all shoe merchants. However, the hon. gentleman used1 the illustration that the shoe merchant in this town was a man who many years ago had been the shoemaker who made the shoes with his hands and sold- them himself. And my hon. friend from Huron North cannot understand why, now that we have modern machinery to make shoes, he still has to pay the same price or a higher price for shoes than when the shoemaker made them by hand. Well, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman will accompany me for a few minutes in the sphere of realism instead of the realm of fiction I shall make one or two suggestions for his consideration.
When the shoe merchant was a shoemaker we had an entirely different standard, of living. In that dlay even the shoemaker's children went to school in their bare feet, in order to save shoes and stockings, as did most of the other children.

I was in me course of outlining some factors which enter into the cost of shoes to-day. I named one. Secondly, in the days when the shoe merchant of today was the shoemaker of yesterday, the shoemaker's wife probably got one new dress a year. To-day the shoe merchant's wife probably gets three or four or five or six new
The Budget-Mr. Lawson

dresses a year. In the days when the shoe merchant was a shoemaker there were no radios, and the shoemaker probably would never have purchased one if there were, whereas to-day they are owned as a necessity, not a luxury, by all workers in the shoe factories that make the shoes which are sold by the shoe merchant. In fact, the shoe merchant of to-day probably never dreamed in the days when he was a shoemaker of owning even a horse and buggy, much less the automobile in which to-day he travels, nor did he dream of having even a secondt-hand Ford such as is possessed by a great majority of the workers in the shoe factories of this country to-day. What does that mean? It simply means that you cannot compare the standard of living of thirty or forty years ago with the standard of living to-day. If the hon. member for Huron North had wanted to put a reasonable proposition to the shoe merchant he might have asked him why it is that a shoe made to-day in a Canadian factory by Canadian workmen with this modern machinery is sold for less money than a shoe made by hand1 to-day as a custom made shoe. Subject to adjustments which undoubtedly should be made in certain industries, never let us forget that we cannot lower costs without lowering wages, and you cannot lower wages without creating more unemployment.
That in turn gives me a thought that I should like to suggest to the Minister of Labour and to this house for consideration. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had something to say on this score during the last election campaign. In speaking at Vancouver on September 30, 1935, according to the reports in the newspapers, the right hon. gentleman set out ten points of the policy of the Liberal party. It will be noted that when the leader of the Conservative party sets out a policy he is always confronted with it as a promise, and then accused of breaking his promises. Let me suggest one point to the Minister of Labour; No. 5 set out by the present Prime Minister in Vancouver was, the democratization of industry by giving labour equal rights with capital in forming industrial policy. I should like to ask the Minister of Labour to tell us to-night what has been done towards implementing that promise and that policy. I suggest to you, sir, and to this house, that if the Minister of Labour had exercised as much effort in accomplishing the purpose declared by his leader as he has in fussing about with his employment commission he probably would have contributed a great deal more to the solution of this country's unemployment problem.

The hon. member for Huron North, again in his speech said concerning the leader of the opposition:
Unemployment gave him his greatest victory, unemployment led to his defeat, and I think it must have been for him a supreme pleasure that he was able to return to this house and review the army of the unemployed which he and his party did so much to create.
Well sir, there may be those who disagree with the policy pursued by the Conservative party during the time they were in power for the solution of the unemployment problem. Undoubtedly there are those who will say that we did not entirely succeed. But I suggest that there are few who would accuse the Conservative party of creating the unemployment problem, having regard to the conditions prevailing in this country when we came into power, and having regard to the economic upheaval which swept the whole world at that time. The hon. member says the leader of the opposition came back to review the army of the unemployed; I should like to suggest that if the employment commission in this country appoints as many more appointees by order in council in the next nine months as it has in the last nine months, the hon. member for Huron North in his field of fiction will have the Minister of Labour going out in the uniform of a little colonel to review that army of employees of the employment commission and to accept the salute from those loyal Liberals who obtained jobs through that medium.
Now I come to the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), who dwelt at great length on the cooperation that existed between this government and the employment commission, and the cooperation this government was receiving from the provinces and municipalities. Well, sir, that language had a familiar ring, so I looked up some of the election speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Sure enough I found that on August 6. 1935, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen the Prime Minister said:
Nationwide cooperation under a national commission in the twin tasks of administering relief and providing work for the unemployed is the policy of the Liberal party on the unemployment question.
Then, a little later, he said:
A program of useful relief works, including slum clearance . . . public buildings, highways, level crossing elimination, preservation of historic sites and other projects was envisioned by the Liberal leader as an outlet for the energies of unemployed Canadians-
Well, Mr. Speaker, where are they all?

Well, I am going to try to give him one or two, though I hope they will not be of such solid concrete that he will not be able to see through them. Why not let us get a little cooperation from the provinces in order to enact those measures of social legislation which are so badly needed and which would provide employment in this country? How well I remember the present Prime Minister going up and, down this country during the last campaign appealing to the people to elect a Liberal government in Canada. In effect he said, "We have Liberal governments in almost all the provinces now, and if you elect us to power at Ottawa we will be one big family. We will all be able to get together and agree." Apparently a tremendous number of electors took him at his word. After he came to power he did call a conference; representatives of the provincial governments

did come to Ottawa and they did agree, but to what? They agreed to get rid of all this social legislation by hoisting it over to the courts for opinions on hypothetical questions, instead of waiting for a concrete case that could be decided on the facts. As a result of the decision of the court it has been determined that the provinces have the power to enact legislation dealing with minimum wages and maximum hours of labour, measures which I am confident even the Minister of Labour will agree would create a great deal of employment in this country if put into force. Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the budget and the amendment. As I study it, I am more than ever convinced that I shall support the amendment moved by the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). As one examines casually the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) it would seem that there has been an endeavour to better conditions, but when one scrutinizes his oration a little more closely, he is compelled to change his mind somewhat. I believe in the dire circumstances in which we find ourselves something greater than endeavours are necessary to alleviate conditions in which due to the depression our people find themselves to-day.
One thing upon which I should like to commend the government is the subvention on coal. If there is one thing which will assist the country I believe it is the furtherance of interprovincial trade. Alberta, from which I come, and concerning which I am more qualified to speak, is one of the greatest coal producing sections of Canada. She needs assistance to enable her to produce and deliver her coal to the east, and to compete with the provinces with which she must compete in the industry. I would go further and say that greater assistance should be given to the coal industry, not to the detriment of the eastern coal producing provinces, but to the advantage of all the provinces concerned.
I am sorry indeed to note that millions of tons of coal are shipped in from Pennsylvania, great quantities from Wales and, as was pointed out the other day, even from Germany. I do not believe it is proper to permit coal to come in from foreign countries, particularly when we are faced with an unemployment problem. The coal is permitted to come in and to compete with coal produced in our own provinces.
I do not believe tariffs will solve our difficulties. In my opinion it does not make much difference whether tariffs are high or low, so long as we do not protect the home market for our own people. Subventions, which the government is continuing, have been recommended by the party in this section of the house to which I belong. We call it a price discount; but no matter what it may be called, the principle remains the same. I believe that any industry should be assisted by bonuses or subventions if it can prove conclusively that 311X1-974
it is in need of assistance. Under such circumstances proper assistance should be given to it.
I should like now to refer to page 1213 of Hansard where the minister refers to the wheat situation in the following language:
With regard to wheat, the 193<i yield was about 52-7 million bushels below that of 1935, and was the smallest crop since 1919. Drought conditions again played havoc in certain areas, destroying crops completely in some districts and reducing to meagre levels the yield in others. In spite of the smaller 1936 yield, however, the value of this crop was substantially above the value of the 1935 crop due to greatly enhanced prices, which are again reaching levels which promise more profitable and stable conditions for the western farmer.
I am glad he put in the words, "which promise." I admit that there is some degree of correctness in that statement, but from the farmer's standpoint it is absolutely untrue. The farmers of western Canada have been living on promises so long that they will not be able to carry on much longer. There is an impression among certain members of this house, as well as throughout eastern Canada, that the western farmer has benefited greatly by the rise in the price of wheat. Those of us who live in the west know only too well that the farmer never receives the top price for his wheat. His financial condition generally forces him to sell his wheat in the fall when the price is at the lowest point. It is not he who makes the profit out of the wheat, it is men, such as the one referred to the other day by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), who make profits of half a million dollars out of wheat operations.

speechtext:
As I said before, because of financial difficulties caused by the orthodox system under which we work, the farmer is compelled to sell his wheat in the early fall and he does not get the top price. It is the speculator working through the grain exchange who buys at the low figure and sells at $1.30 a bushel. Had these farmers been given participation certificates they could have shared in the profits made. The farmers would have been in a much better position, and such a step would have gone a long way towards solving our unemployment problem. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) pointed out quite clearly that the farmers have not been getting a sufficient share of the profit. At page 1213 of Hansard he is reported as follows:
Since that time, however, prices have greatly improved, particularly in the past year, and by the end of 193C this index had moved up to 32-4 of the 1926 level. While prices of things which the farmer sells have been moving upward, there has been relatively little change in the prices of things which he buys. In fact, taking 1926 prices as equal to 100, we find the retail price index in December, 1936, standing at 81-8, while, as noted above, prices of agricultural products had reached the 82.4 level after a rapid rise in the last few months of the year. At the end of 1936, therefore, the farmer's relative position, as far as prices were concerned, was slightly better than in 1926. Wide disparity between prices of primary and finished products is perhaps the most significant feature of what we call a depression, and it is greatly to be hoped that this approximate parity between agricultural and other prices can be maintained.
It certainly is greatly to be hoped that this approximate parity between agricultural and other prices can be maintained. These figures show that the position of the farmer in 1936 is approximately 20 per cent below what it

was in 1926. How do you expect the farmers of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to meet their present obligations when they must produce approximately 20 per cent more to meet those obligations? Had the government been a little more considerate and permitted the farmers to have these participation certificates, the farmers would have been much better off. This is one more instance of how the west has been discriminated against. There certainly has been an increase in business, but I would not say that has benefited the western farmer.
There is one other question I should like to deal with before I sit down. This is something of which we have heard a great deal in this house, but it is always referred to very guardedly. I have in mind the financial position of certain of the western provinces. I do not mean to be sarcastic when I say that this question is treated much too lightly; it is more serious than many of us realize, and the results may be more disastrous than we expect. During the last two or three weeks I have received many letters protesting against what is considered the discriminatory attitude of this government towards the west. I should like to read one letter which I received only to-day, and which is a sample of the many I have received lately. This will give the house some idea of what the people in western Canada are thinking. I might mention that I have received letters from Saskatchewan, Manitoba, British Columbia as well as from Alberta. The following was received from Alberta:
At a regular meeting held by the above group, the following resolution was made and carried:
"'That this group go on record protesting the obvious discrimination shown by the federal government against Alberta in regards to financial and relief matters."
I do not think there is any doubt, at least in the minds of many people in the western provinces, that there has been discrimination shown by this government.
If this idea prevails widely, it may result in very grave consequences. In regard to this particular question I wish to quote from Hansard, page 1214:
It is unfortunately true, however, that the financial position of several of our provincial governments is such that they are unable to take advantage of prevailing low interest rates in order either to reduce their fixed charges by refunding outstanding debt or to obtain new funds for relief or other expenditures. Despite drastic efforts to reduce expenditures and increase taxes, and despite a long record of honourable dealing


The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
I hope that remark was made in all seriousness, and I believe it was.
-with their creditors, they have been unable either to balance their budgets or to have recourse to the investment market for the funds necessary to meet their commitments.
This is- a problem to which the government has given the most serious and unremitting attention since the day it assumed office. I need not recount the efforts which were made last year to find a solution. The plan then evolved which would have made low rates available to the provinces as a result of dominion assistance under appropriate safeguards, proved unacceptable in several quarters. The acute stage which the problem has reached in Manitoba and Saskatchewan during the recent past_ led the government to make the decision which was announced by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the house last week.
The question is being asked, and I think rightly, why is Alberta being discriminated against? Manitoba and Saskatchewan were assisted by this government, but Alberta was not.

speechtext:
The fact that the other two western provinces were assisted would lead people to believe that Alberta was discriminated against. Whether
intentionally or not is not the point at issue. But I think it is quite obvious that that is one of the circumstances which have led the people to believe that there was gross discrimination. A moment ago I read one of the many resolutions in that regard that I have received. Not only are the people as individuals in the three prairie provinces, and1 in British Columbia also, discussing this question, but the press is taking it up. The other day I cut out an article in a western paper, the Calgary Albertan of Saturday, February 20, 1937, entitled, very appropriately, An Ace in the Hole:
The great oil resources of this province have proved to be Alberta's ace in the hole. For the benefit of the uninformed it may be explained that an ace in the hole is an unexpos-ed playing card of that rank which, in a stud poker game, often comes in handy. Recent developments in Turner Valley should convince all people that if there is one part of Canada which has the assets on -which credit may be properly and safely founded that place is Alberta.
Neither the scolding nor the sophistries of the financial spokesmen, journalistic and otherwise, can obscure that fact. There is no doubt that at the time Alberta requested aid from the dominion government for the purpose o' paying interest and avoiding default this province was entitled to assistance both as a matter of business and as a matter of equity.
I should like to emphasize that-"as a matter of business and as a matter of equity."
It could not and cannot be seriously asserted that the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba are entitled to better -treatment than Alberta from the standpoint of possession of assets. These are the firmest bases for credit.
But someone is sure to say that Alberta has been discriminated against because of its Social Credit government. That is doubtless stating the true situation. But it only makes the discrimination more shockingly unjust. If a government is to be penalized because it is engaged in an earnest and honest endeavour-
And in -the minister's budget speech he said they had made an honest attempt:
-to restore hope and prosperity to Alberta, then it is none too soon to let all men know it'.
It is refreshing to note that Right Honourable R. B. Bennett has publicly stated that Alberta has been discriminated against. The Albertan may not agree with all or many of Mr. Bennett's ideas, but we hasten to admit that on more than one occasion it has been constrained to admire his trong sense of justice. It cannot be said that Mr. Bennett is a Social Crediter, or at least he has not yet indicated it. But he objects, as many others do, to Alberta receiving unfair treatment because it turned out a government of which it was thoroughly weary and supplanted it overwhelmingly with a new one.
All Albertans believe that Alberta should have fair play.
That is all they ask, Mr. Speaker, that Alberta be fairly treated; and the people are determined that they shall get at least justice.
1540	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
From the point of view of the assets of the province of Alberta there should be no doubt in the mind of anyone that that province should be given greater assistance than any other in the dominion. Alberta is one of the leading wheat producing provinces, one of the leading coal producing provinces, and the dominion's leading oil producing province; I will go further, and say that her actual and potential oil production is the greatest in the British Empire. That asset alone in time of war, as to which we are all so greatly concerned, should make it important to every member of parliament and every Canadian citizen that assistance be given for the development of that industry. I am told by very well informed men that financial institutions in eastern Canada are seriously hindering or endeavouring to hinder its progress.
Some may say that it is because Alberta has a Social Credit government; in fact some hon. members have already said so. I refer hon. members to page 985 of Hansard, to a statement made by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh). For the sake of continuity I will read the preceding paragraph:
Mr. Bennett:	If the hon. gentleman will
permit me, that statement happens to be inaccurate-although I am bound to accept it-Alberta was driven to default, and people holding its bonds have in some cases been practically ruined because of the inability of that province to pay. The Minister of Finance would not help Alberta although it asked for help, and now the other two provinces are to be helped.
Then the hon. member for North Battleford said:
In answer to the statement made by the leader of the opposition I would say that if Alberta is seeing evil days financially and industrially the fault does not lie _ with the dominion government, the finance minister, or the Prime Minister of this country. It lies very largely with Alberta, headed by the government existing in that province at the present time.
That is the impression which is being given. We in Canada take pride in our democracy; our government is elected by the people. I say, therefore, that any dominion government that discriminates against a particular province because of its government, a government elected by the people of that province, takes an altogether wrong attitude, and the people of the west are resenting it most strenuously. Surely the time has come for us to take a broader view of things than the view which this government has taken of the situation in Alberta. When hon. members get up and defend the attitude of the government it is time for us to consider the question seriously. The people of Alberta elected their government by an overwhelming majority, one of the largest

in history. They were not to blame for the debt that was created by other governments. I do not necessarily suggest that the other governments created that debt intentionally; nevertheless that was the condition of the province when they were in power. The present government of Alberta was elected by the people to help them and that is what that government is doing, and the people of that province are more determined than ever, and justly so, to see that they get fair play.
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln) : I desire at this time to make a few general observations on the amendment before the house. First may I refer in part to a statement I made last year when I opposed the appointment of the National Employment Commission. I opposed it then and I still oppose it in principle to-day, especially when its accomplishments have been reviewed and the matter has been fully considered. In part I said at that time: We have a bill before us which has for its purpose the setting up of a national employment commission. What purpose can be served when we consider the dire necessity that faces many of our Canadian citizens? What is this commission to do? Is it to review the statistics already compiled by one authority or another, or is it just another way of spending money to no good purpose?
My claim was that the urgent need of the day was to protect the lives and ideals of our Canadian people. That need is even greater to-day than it was at that time. The generation of young voters that has come into being, those who voted in 1935, are still talking about the conspicuous posters that were emblazoned across Canada, and I frequently hear them referring to one in particular. It has often been referred to in this house, the one we were all particularly interested in, which predicted the beneficial effects that would come from voting for the Liberal party-"Vote Liberal and End Unemployment."	.
It has often been said here that unemployment is a question of paramount importance; that has been acknowledged by the Prime Minister and every member of the house. Challenges have been made to the leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King), and when I pointed out last year what the government had promised, hon. members across the floor said "hear, hear" and declared that the promise that had been made would be carried out. I ask now, to what extent has that promise been fulfilled? Someone may say at once, "Has there not been an increase

The Budget-Mr. Lockhart
in the number of those absorbed into industry?" Very true; I agree that there has been, but it has been only to a very small extent. I am quite sure the statistics will bear out that statement. We find, however, that as a whole throughout Canada unemployment has increased by approximately 100,000.
Let us turn to the increase in trade with Great Britain since 1932. That was a definite accomplishment of the late government, and a statement of this remarkable increase has already been placed on Hansard. Every newspaper in the country has been lauding the efforts and accomplishments of the late government and there is no need to repeat it here. Our home markets were preserved and with slowly improving world conditions-Canada was enjoying her full measure of that prosperity, perhaps even greater than any other nation in proportion to population. To-day, however, young Canadians are asking all the time when they may expect a fuller measure of the benefits from that growth of trade. But, I repeat, unemployment is on the increase. These young Canadians, young voters of whom I have spoken, continue to point to the subsidies that are being given by the government to steamship companies, railways, western farmers, and in many other directions. Many of them are very worthy, but the younger generation can scarcely understand the vast subsidies that are being given, and they ask, and rightly so, "When are the wage earners to be given their just share and to find a greater demand for their labours?" Surely this is a pertinent question to-day when we are spending millions in various ways. There is apparently a tendency to spend money easily and that is something that perplexes the youth of 1937.
It has been pointed out clearly in this house that after the western farmer has been aided in the purchase of fine seed grain, and in many other ways, he has been deprived of his rightful share of the increasing profits from the wheat he has grown. This government has so manipulated the sale of the farmer's wheat that he has never realized on the increased prices paid in foreign markets, these profits having found their way into the pockets of private speculators. That statement also is spread on Hansard in detail, and I do not intend to enlarge upon it. At any rate I do not hear from hon. members any contradiction of the statement that on the whole the struggling farmer was sold out, whereas we do hear a good deal about the private interests. In all the newspapers, both from the west and from the east,
we are told how the farmers' wheat was sold at a sacrifice, the profits going into other private pockets, through what might be called illegitimate channels.
Is that a good way to get the confidence of the Canadian people, and particularly the younger generation, who are perturbed in many ways and wondering what this is all about? Is it not playing into the hands of the disturbing influences that we have heard so much about and the many elements which we are told1 are undermining the very democracy of which we are proud. Is it not undermining the ideals and ambitions of our young Canada? Only this week I received a strong protest from a young Canadian farmer in Saskatchewan who was formerly in my employ. I quote this as an illustration of how this may work out in practice.
He was a keen and ambitious young man; he served overseas for four years and was one of the few who came back unmarked. He decided! to take up a quarter section in Saskatchewan, of land allotted to returned1 soldiers who qualified. He pioneered, as those we have heard so much about in the early days. I have often heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) speak of the pioneer days of the west. This young man went through similar experiences. He lived in a shack built by his own hands; for several years he laboured early and late; he saved his money, bought more land, and built himself a small comfortable farmer's home. He married1 and has a small family. Along with thousands more he was obliged to sacrifice his wheat, which went into the hands of private speculators who, assisted by the present government, were in a position to capitalize on the farmer's necessities. He did not realize enough from, his grain to keep solvent, and this week I have received a letter saying that he has given up in despair and intends to move as soon as he can gather his few belongings together, to the United States and start anew. Another good Canadian gone, broken in spirit. Is it any wonder he writes in bitter condemnation of being sold out and his just earnings diverted into private hands? It takes a lot of courage and conviction for a young man to retain his morale after going through such an experience and coming out at the short end.
I think this whole position was very clearly dealt with by the leader of the opposition, and I have not heard anyone contradict the statements he made in moving his amendment. People talk of immigration, when we blot out the lives almost of Canadians who have pioneered and who have a right to a place in Canadian life. I lay such instances at the door of the present government, and I
The Budget-Mr. Lockhart

venture to say that many hon. members could testify to experiences of that kind. There is surely a day of reckoning coming, if we deal with young Canadian life in that manner.
I again remind the government that unemployment is the paramount question of the day. We hear rumours of relief camps being again established1. Surely with improving conditions we are not going back to the distress of those former days! Surely two years of study of unemployment by duplicating statistical departments should have convinced any government by this time that the amount of money already spent by the National Employment Commission is spent to no advantage. It provides merely a duplication of statistical records. Our young Canadian manhood and womanhood are sick and tired of statistics. Their whole cry is that they want work, and more work, pay envelopes and more pay envelopes. No wonder they are cynical when they discuss the present home improvement plan.
I had the privilege recently of being asked to act on the executive in connection with the administration of this plan. It is a worthy piece of legislation; I am quite satisfied it is good legislation, and I heartily endorse this effort of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). On the other hand, how can a man without a job apply to any lending institution for a loan of a paltry few hundred dollars to repair his home when the first qualification he must have is a job? No wonder he is critical. No wonder at times these young people come to us and scoff.
In the presentation of the Canada-United Kingdom trade agreement I consider that too much stress is laid on foreign trade, and that our home markets are being overlooked. Scores of small towns and urban municipalities are dependent on small industries such as textiles, which produce steady pay-rolls for their people. Surely it is apparent that reduced protection to this industry will have far-reaching effects. Recent inquiries have revealed that many textile mills are even now finding it difficult to carry on. If their home markets are further invaded one of two results is bound to follow; either wages will be reduced and the standard of living be lowered, or many of these mills will go out of business. Canada has seen this happen before.
The fabricated steel industry of this country should also be better protected. I have some knowledge of that industry, although not engaged in it myself. Why can we not help ;his industry to expand in Canada, instead jf passing prohibitory measures which only curtail its operations?

The Minister of Finance is to be commended for his efforts to reestablish the building trades and increase employment in that direction. I think, however, that his estimate of the proportion of labour employed in the building trades and in the manufacture of building material was considerably lower than is actually the case. The production of steel in all its forms should be one of our largest secondary industries. It plays a most important part in the construction of homes and buildings of the larger types. Sheet metal could and should be manufactured in Canada, and no restraint should be placed on production of this kind.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am in favour of expansion of our foreign markets providing that is not done at the expense of our home markets and our basic and secondary industries. Nations can change their foreign policies overnight, as we have seen happen so often in the past. We do not want to wake up some morning and find that our home markets have been sacrificed, but I am definitely of the opinion that this is being done by the lower protection that is proposed.
I strongly criticize the apparent neglect by the government of the unemployment situation which exists in Canada, and the apparent decrease in opportunities for employment. I heartily endorse the amendment proposed by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and I think hon. members would be well advised to consider the far reaching effects of the lower protection that is being afforded our basic and secondary industries. I feel that the youth of the country are disappointed because they realize the possibility that our home markets will be invaded and their chances of securing employment thereby be lessened instead of increased. I hope many hon. members on the government side will express themselves on this question, because I know there are those in the house who have had the same experiences I have had, and we all hope that our industries and our citizens will be protected to the fullest possible extent.
