speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the address of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in the course of which he moved an amendment to the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). When the right hon. gentleman moved that amendment I had the feeling that probably he did not think he was quite doing justice to the government. At that time he knew that the only real policy he attempted to apply in

The Budget-Mr. Tucker
the solution of the problem of unemployment was that of raising tariffs, and he knew that policy had failed. He knew that he had spent five years in endeavouring to cure unemployment in Canada, and he knew that only sixteen months had passed during which this government had an opportunity of applying its policies. He knew very well that it takes time to get policies in operation and more time for them to have the ultimate effect expected. So I have no doubt that when the right hon. gentleman moved his amendment he realized that it was really too early to condemn a government which had been in power only sixteen months, when he had failed after five years.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend more or less attempted to justify himself by saying, in effect: "I am moving this amendment because it is the same amendment with which I was met when I was at the head of the government." I submit that moving a motion such as this when the policies which you are condemning are failing is very different from moving a similar motion when apparently those policies are succeeding. So it seemed to me that the right hon. leader of the opposition felt that perhaps he was not doing just the right thing by the present government in moving his amendment.
In that connection, and especially in view of the remarks of the preceding speaker (Mr. Lockhart), I think it is only fair to go back to the figures disclosed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in his speech on this amendment. According to the right hon. leader of the opposition the number of unemployed in this country when he assumed office was 117,000. When he left office there were 435,000 unemployed, but in October last that number had been reduced to 392,000. In other words, there has been a reduction since this government has been in office. I was glad that the Minister of Labour did not pretend to be satisfied with what had been accomplished, but merely said that the improvement was such as to give hope and confidence. As far as this country is concerned I think it feels that since coming into office the present government has applied itself unremittingly and faithfully to the solution of the various problems confronting it, and I think the country at large really feels that more has been accomplished by this government in sixteen months than was accomplished in a similar time by any other government that occupied the treasury benches of this country since confederation. When I say that I do not pretend that I agree with all that has been done by this government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman says he voted against the government at times. Perhaps I may do the same thing if my conscience compels me to do so. No, Mr. Speaker; as I say, it may be that in some matters I should have liked to see the government adopt different policies or go further in certain directions, but I do not believe that anyone should expect any government to do everything that each private member would like it to do. After all, Mr. Speaker, all any member can expect of any government is that on the whole it should be doing, as he thinks, fairly well, making as few mistakes as a government can be expected to make.
A great deal has been said, for example, in regard to what the government has done concerning wheat. I know many hon. members who have had a good deal to say about wheat who had nothing to say when the western farmer was selling his wheat for 21 cents a bushel. But to-d-ay, when the farmer is getting over a dollar a bushel, these members are weeping crocodile tears over his plight. The people of this country and the farmers take note of these things, and they are not misled by this late concern for their interests. They do not forget all that has happened since 1930. I will deal with the government's wheat marketing policy later on.
The hon. member who just spoke, together with many of those who have taken part in the debate on behalf of the official opposition, suggested that by the small tariff reductions being made by this government the home market was in some way not being preserved, so that unemployment will be increased.
Since it has been incorporated, the Dominion Textile Company has made on an average 97 per cent on the investment in its common shares. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if the Dominion Textile Company had been forced by lower tariffs, and the competition it would have had to face on account of lower tariffs, to charge less for the goods which it produced, would it not have sold
The Budget-Mr. Tucker

more of those goods, and would it not have promoted more employment as a result? Would it not have been better if the Dominion Textile Company had sold its goods cheaper, and sold perhaps twice as much to the people who needed the goods, instead of making 97 per cent profit for the promoters, on the common shares? Would it not have been better if it had distributed some of those millions of dollars to the working people of this country, about whom the official opposition pretend to be so much concerned?

speechtext:
May I say that this has been the second budget speech to which I have had the opportunity to listen. I felt it was a most complete review of the financial situation of Canada and most understandable to any person even one who is not an expert in financial matters.
I was particularly pleased with the introduction of pensions for the blind. I felt that it was altogether fitting that an administration headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should have introduced such a system, in view of the fact that it was his administration which introduced the system of old age pensions. I notice that in the appropriations for the Old Age Pensions Act the estimated expenditures for the next fiscal year are placed at $22,500,000, which means that apparently it is expected there will be at least 112.000 old people who will benefit by the act in the coming year. Knowing of some of the suffering that prevails now and has prevailed during the last five or six years I think every hon. member must have been grateful on many occasions to know that an Old Age Pensions Act is in force, and has been in force during those years of suffering and hardship. I believe one of the things for which the present Prime Minister will be gratefully remembered is that he introduced in this Parliament one of the first measures providing for

The Budget-Mr. Tucker
social security for those unable to take care of themselves. I have no doubt that already many thousands of old people have gone to their last reward, having enjoyed a much happier evening of life than they would have but for the action of the administration headed1 by the present Prime Minister in establishing a system of Old Age Pensions.
Similarly, in connection with pensions for the blind, supported as they were by all parties, I am sure every hon. member was delighted that it was deemed possible to introduce the measure at this session. Presumably it will benefit at least 2,000 people who, after all, have enough handicaps to face without having the extra one of not being sure of at least a bare subsistence.
I do not intend now to discuss in detail schedules in the budget, but there is one point which strikes me and it is this, that while not destroying a reasonable amount of protection (and many will still regard as unreasonable the protection left-the protection is still so high that even the official opposition should regard it as reasonable) by introducing a certain amount of competition from old country textiles, the textile people in Canada will be forced to reduce their prices so that people who have just come through the depression will be able to buy more goods, thereby increasing the general wellbeing of the poor people of Canada. Employment will be increased', and no one, with the exception of those people who have had exorbitant profits in the past, will be injured.
How anybody can condemn a budget like that is more than I can understand. The only condemnation that I would have of it is that it leaves far too much protection for those people who to-day, we are told, are going to be forced to the wall because they cannot get along with a thirty per cent protection. I submit that if there is an industry in Canada that has to have a protection of thirty per cent or more in order to exist, it is uneconomical and an absolute burden to Canada. It would be a great deal better if the capital invested1 in that industry were put into another industry economically sound, one which would provide more labour, and contribute to the general well being.
To find out how the tariff actually works out I looked into a few items, one of which was blankets. On December 30, 1936, a shipment of blankets weighing 1,226 pounds and worth $590, entered this country. The tariff was 22^ per cent less 10 per cent if the goods came through empire ports, so the ad valorem duty was $119.48. There was a specific duty of 10 cents per pound, less 10 per cent, which amounted to $110.34 on these blankets. This
meant that this shipment of blankets worth $590 paid a duty of $229.82, or 39 per cent upon an ad valorem basis. Under the new tariff the ad valorem rate is 20 per cent, less 10 per cent, which amounts to $106.20. The specific rate is 5 cents per pound, less 10 per cent, which amounts to $55.17, or a total of $161.37. Worked out on an ad valorem basis, this amounts to 27-35 per cent. In other words, the tariff on blankets has been reduced from 39 to 27-35 per cent.
For every $100 worth of blankets, the manufacturers in this country can still charge $127. They can charge $27 more than would be charged if there was no tariff. I submit that in connection with a necessity like blankets, if the manufacturer in this country is not able to function with the natural tariff imposed by the cost of shipping the goods from another country, plus this 27 per cent, then the industry should not exist. Anything beyond that is too much of a burden upon the consuming people of this country, especially in connection with a necessity like blankets.
Let me refer to a shipment of five dozen woollen socks, valued at $8, which came in on November 7, 1936. The duty was 30 per cent ad valorem, less 10 per cent, which amounted to $2.16. The specific duty was 75 cents per dozen, less 10 per cent, which amounted to $3.38. The total duty on those $8 worth of socks under the old tariff was $5.54. Under the new budget, the ad valorem rate will be 20 per cent, less 10 per cent, or $1.44. The specific rate will be 30 cents per dozen, less 10 per cent, or $1.35. This makes a total duty of $2.79. Worked out on an ad valorem basis, the previous duty was 69 per cent, a rather high duty on an article which is absolutely necessary in this country. This is the sort of duty that was imposed in order that our textile barons could make almost 100 per cent on their money. Under the new tariff the ad valorem rate is 34-87 per cent. When my friends of the opposition cry out because a duty is too low at 34-87 per cent, I wonder how much they really care about the consumers of this country. If they were saying that that duty was too high, that it should be lowered still more in order that more goods might be bought and employment increased, then I might be able to sympathize with them in their argument. But when they condemn the budget because prices are going to be reduced and employment increased, and then move an amendment to the effect that the government is not curing unemployment fast enough, I cannot follow their reasoning.
There is another matter in connection with the budget to which I should like to
The Budget-Mr. Tucker

refer. It should not be forgotten that when the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) came into power in 1930 Great Britain was still a free trade country. He went over to England and suggested that that country should change its tariff policy and give a preference to Canadian goods by putting on a tariff against foreign goods. That suggestion was treated with scorn by the government of that day in Great Britain. The leader of the opposition then suggested that Great Britain might be at the parting of the ways. There was a hint there; and then that if England did not adopt the tariff policy which the right hon. gentleman, then Prime Minister of this country, suggested to them, it might not be so good for trade relations within the empire.
The British people listened to the opinion of that eminent statesman, and who knows but what that opinion may have had something to do with causing England to be no longer a free trade country. England became a protectionist country when she adopted the policy suggested by the leader of the opposition. In fact, I believe the party of which he is the head took a great deal of credit to themselves because for the first time in history we had a market open to us in Great Britain which was closed to other countries by means of a tariff.

speechtext: Not closed.

speechtext:
Partially closed by a tariff. They took credit for that situation, but I ask you: Was it something for which they should take credit? What was the situation? The farmers of Great Britain obtained a certain amount of protection against the foodstuffs of foreign countries, but they obtained none against the food products of the dominions. What was the attitude of the farmens in Great Britain? It must be known to every member of this house that the farmers began to take the attitude that as British manufacturers were protected, they the farmers, should also be protected against empire as well as foreign food products. They contended that as the dominions had put on a tariff against the main products of Great Britain they should have a tariff against the food products of the dominions. Our right to free access to the British market was endangered, and always will be endangered while England is on that basis. For the first time she was no longer a free trade country.
The same thing was true when the present government came to negotiate the new treaty. The people of the United Kingdom began to realize that through the Ottawa agreements we had increased our sales tremendously in

the United Kingdom, but we had not given them entry to our market to nearly the same extent. The argument was used that if Canada was going to deal on that unfair basis, then they wanted protection against the food products of Canada. They began to argue for protection against Canadian hams, bacon and wheat to the same extent as they were protected against the food products of foreign countries.
I do not think there is any doubt that if we are not very careful we may lose our preference in that great market. Why? Because of the very thing over which the official opposition boasted, that they had got England to adopt a different fiscal policy. What was this government faced with? They had to go to England and say to the British government: We will give you concessions in order that you may be able to justify your not protecting your own farmers against our food products. The farmers of Great Britain contended that if the manufacturers of that country were protected, they should also be protected. I presume it was pretty hard for the government of Great Britain to deny a certain measure of protection to their farmers. Therefore, we had to offer a much better deal to the British government than that held out by the right hon. leader of the opposition.
But we profit by that deal. If we lower the tariff on goods coming into this country, prices are lowered to the consumers. It means that more of those goods will be purchased. If there remains some protection to the producers of these goods, it means that more will be made and sold in this country, and the result will be that we shall have benefited in several ways, by preserving our markets in Great Britain, by increasing employment at home, and by enlarging our ability to enjoy more of the goods upon which these tariffs are lowered. That is the situation in regard to the tariff as I see it. There is no doubt that the agreement was received with great gratification, especially by the farmers of this country. For example, here is a statement made by Mr. H. B. Cowan, secretary of the Canadian Dairy Farmers' Federation, representing 150,000 organized dairy farmers. He said:
It is gratifying to farmers that the Canadian overnment has reached such an important and avourable agreement. National farmers' unions of the United Kingdom backed by strong Conservative support in the British house have been urging imposition of levies and quotas on imports of farm products, and the government there issued a white paper almost committing it to this policy. Farmer organizations in Canada and the other dominions have contacted their governments to combat that policy.

The Budget-Mr. Tucker
The opportunity to ship into that market
280,000.000 pounds of bacon and ham in the next three years should give us, in view of the fact that we have used in the past roughly only one-half of that quota at any time, a chance to expand that production tremendously. Will anybody say that that is not something worth while? The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) may say that under the treaties which he negotiated we had that right. But I submit that because those treaties were so one-sided-and the official opposition are inclined to take credit for driving such a good deal-because it was such a "good deal," although really, through its ultimate results, a bad deal-this government should be heartily congratulated upon overcoming the handicaps they had to meet in the hostility of many interests in the United Kingdom owing to the one-sided way that the Ottawa treaties have worked out, and upon getting such a favourable treaty for this country.
One of the speakers for the official opposition referred this evening to the fact that the present government when in opposition objected that there were still certain items on which the preference was bound. But it should not be forgotten that in the treaty negotiated by the present leader of the opposition there were 215 such items, and that that number has been reduced by the present government to 91. The opposition may inquire, why did you agree even to 91 items? After all, we all admit that it takes two to make an agreement, and that when the United Kingdom had an absolutely guaranteed preference on 215 items, it was quite an achievement to get that number reduced to 91. I submit, as well as hope, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of our power to lower the tariff on those items which have been dropped from the bound list, it will now be possible for us to negotiate once more with the president of the neighbouring republic and get an even better treaty with Washington than we got last year. Through this agreement with the United Kingdom the foundation has been laid for extending the United States trade agreement from which we have already benefited so much. That is another reason why I intend to vote against this amendment and for the budget resolution.
There is another matter with which at the moment I should like to deal because it is one in which I, as one of the younger members of this house, am very much interested. We hear a great deal, and properly so, from hon. members representing the central provinces about their unemployed young people. We have unemployed young people whom I would
designate as the forgotten young people of Canada. They are not on any unemployment relief list. They cannot come under a farm placement scheme. Their ages range from fifteen to thirty years. Their parents do not need them any longer at home, but they remain there because there they get food and shelter. The young men and young women of western Canada are staying in their parents' homes long past the time when they should be out establishing homes of their own.
A very competent observer of Saskatchewan conditions told me to-day that in his opinion there are at least 50,000 young men in Saskatchewan from eighteen or nineteen to thirty years of age who are staying with their parents and for whom there is no real work, who cannot get married and establish homes of their own; at the same time, naturally, there is roughly the same number of young women in the same position. When we pay as much as we do for tariff protection, which helps people who live near these protected industries in central Canada, we should be willing to do something to give our young people the chance to get settled and started in life. We hear something of immigration policies. I submit that this government should set aside a certain sum of money from which a young man wishing to start up for himself and establish a home should be able to apply for a reasonable loan, which he should receive provided he can show he has a piece of land that he can go on with a reasonable hope of making a success. That loan should be repayable at a low rate of interest over a long period of time. If that were done it would enable several thousands of our young men to settle on their own land, get married, establish homes, and begin to raise families the way their fathers did before them. Seeing that Canadian governments have spent millions of dollars in past years in bringing in immigrants from other countries, to-day we should, I submit, have enough vision and imagination to spend some money to settle and give a start to young people who were bom in this country, and who are the best settlers we can have. When it is suggested that we spend money on cooperative schemes to bring strangers to our shores from other countries-I care not where they come from- I say that before we fetch anybody in from outside we should look after our own boys and girls who want to make a start in this country.
I congratulate this government upon its decision to appoint a commission to investigate dominion and provincial relationships. I suggest most seriously, though, that that commission should have the power to investigate
The Budget-Mr. Tucker

the question of tariffs. A great deal has been said in this house about the tariff. One hon. member belonging to the official opposition asked how long were Ontario and Quebec going to remain a pair of placid milk cows to be stripped dry to pay the bills of provincial governments over whose expenditures they had no control? He referred to the provincial governments of the west in making that remark, one which, I submit, was not justified by the facts. I would say that in view of the fact-and I intend if I have time to prove it-that we have been feeding these two milch cows we should have a right to do a little bit of the milking. The Nova Scotia government had a royal commission investigating its relationship to the dominion. It got the present Minister of Labour, who was at that time I believe a professor-an eminent professor-in one of our universities, to prepare a submission to that royal commission on its behalf. As he was at that time appearing for Nova Scotia, not for western Canada, I do not suppose he was trying particularly to make out a case for Saskatchewan, Alberta or Manitoba. He examined into the question of the benefit and injury done by the tariff to the various provinces of this country. That was for the year 1931. I should like to give a few of the figures to the house. He found that the estimated amount of the tariff subsidy to protected manufacturers in Quebec was SI32,867,447, that being 31 * 23 per cent of the benefit from the tariff. He found that the estimated tariff subsidy to manufacturers in Ontario was $220,722,484, Ontario benefiting to the extent of 58-88 per cent. Saskatchewan, with over 900,000 people, almost one-tenth of the population of this dominion, benefited to what extent? Not one per cent, no; it was -77 per cent-S3.275.950. And he found that this tariff subsidy per capita was as follows: Quebec, $46.23, Ontario $64.32 and Saskatchewan $3.55.
We have a few manufacturers in western Canada, but it is interesting to see how little Saskatchewan benefited by the tariff. He gave a table of the net loss or net gain. He found that in one year the province of Saskatchewan paid in extra prices on account of the tariff $29,228,285. He found that it benefited by the tariff to the amount of $3,275,000 as I have already said; in other words, that the tariff cost Saskatchewan in one year, 1931, $25,909,790, or $28.16 per capita. The amount the provincial government collected from our people that year was, I believe, less than $14,000,000, and this tariff subsidy cost our people in one year over $25,000,000. I submit that the year 1931 may be taken as a normal

year; and if you multiply $25,000,000 lost in one year by, let us say, five years, you have the tariff costing Saskatchewan alone since 1931-

I thought I said that, but perhaps I did not. I understood the right hon. gentleman to say that the members of the present government had supported the suggestion that we should have followed sterling when England went off the gold standard. I submit that in fairness to the primary producers we should have done that very thing. By virtue of the fact that we refused to follow sterling, which was our natural market, and instead followed more or less the United States dollar, the growers of wheat in western Canada lost in 1931 $3,469,000. That was the loss to the western wheat growers alone. What all the primary producers lost I do not know; I have not the figures. In 1932 the western wheat growers lost $24,664,000; in 1933 they lost $6,747,000; or a total in those three years of $34,880,000. Why did) we lose that money? Because it was deemed a good thing that we should keep our money as near as possible on a par with United States money so that the government and the financial interests of Canada would not be embarrassed in making payments in the United) States. For that reason the primary producer of Canada was penalized to the extent of millions of dollars, the western wheat grower alone suffering to the extent of $34,880,000. Had we followed Australia, which is a great primary producing nation, had we, like them, considered the interests of the primary producer as being of

The Budget-Mr. Tucker
greater importance than the interests of the financial institutions, in the years from 1900 to 1936 inclusive, the western wheat growers instead of receiving $882,970,000 for their wheat, as they did, would have received $1,112,402,-
000.	Hadi we followed the policy of Australia, which had some compassion on its primary producers, we should have given the western wheat producers $229,432,000 more for their wheat than they got.

May I say in conclusion, however, that any remarks I have made are not intended as a complaint against other parts of Canada. What I am trying to impress upon the house is this: that if the dominion is to be happy in its confederation of provinces; if the provinces are to be content to remain in that confederation; if they are going to work together in that unity and harmony which are essential to make any nation great, then justice has to be done to each part of the dominion. And I lay these facts before the house in answer to the suggestion that western Canada is getting more than it is entitled to. I submit that if you consider our troubles in recent

years and the amounts which we have been

speechtext:
Permit me to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who presented to us what I might call a budget of hope. His statement regarding the present financial position of our country gave rise among our Canadian people to a deep feeling of confidence in better days.
While the international situation is one of the factors of our economic recovery, we must noit forget that the Liberal administration has had much to do with the satisfactory results which we are now witnessing. I have not the slightest intention of analyzing this whole situation; I shall deal with only two questions of local importance, but both are relevant to that intricate problem of unemployment to which our active Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is giving very particular attention.
For some years northwestern Quebec has been making great strides. Towns and villages are growing in the mining districts of Abitibi, and the greatest activity is being displayed especially in the country around the great lake Chibougamau. I have not the latest figures before me, but I can assert that the new mines in that district are employing now almost 10,000 people and are producing millions in gold and copper. It is needless to emphasize further the amazing progress of Abitibi.
Unfortunately, beside this comforting picture there appears a shadow. The trade of the district, amounting to more than $15,000,000 this year, instead of going towards its natural centre of attraction, namely Montreal, is directed rather towards Ontario's metropolis, Toronto. No wonder, Mr. Speaker, that the city of Toronto is about to outclass Montreal in the economic rating of our Canadian cities. There is no better chart of our economic life and no better evidence of the deficiencies of our distribution system. Abitibi absolutely needs an outlet towards the Quebec centres. A road is being built the cost of which will be borne in equal shares by the Quebec and dominion governments, but this road will not be sufficient to ensure a continuous outlet to Montreal for Abitibi's traffic. What we need is a railway. Several attempts have been made in that direction, and more or less earnest promoters have made surveys of the district. If I am correctly informed, in 1910 the dominion govlMr. Tucker.]
ernment went so far as to purchase from Mr. Clergue of Aylmer right of way for a railway to run from Mont Laurief towards the Senneterre district. Later the Northern Railway Company applied for a charter; then came the Abitibi Southern Railway, which also applied for a charter and then let it lapse. To-day we have the Goldfields Transportation Company endeavouring to secure a provincial charter to build a railway from Mont Laurier to Senneterre, to run parallel to the road to which I have already referred.
We are complaining of the heavy deficits of the Canadian National Railways, which constitute an enormous liability in our annual budget. One of the most efficient means of doing away with those deficits would be to build paying lines. I respectfully submit to this house that without further delay the government should advance the necessary funds to enable the Canadian National Railways to build a line from St. Remi d'Amherst to Mont Laurier and from there to the Great Lake-Chibougamau district, through Ferme Neuve, Mt. St. Michel and St. Anne du Lac parishes. This railway would serve four parishes which are being rapidly developed, and would afford an opportunity for settlement in those tracts which are now included within the timber limits of the International Paper Company, more particularly along the Piscatousin river. Investigations have shown that this area contains excellent farming land. Moreover, this railway would become an appreciable source of income for our federal railway system, for all the traffic from the mines now operating in the Chibougamau district would pass over this road.
May I be permitted to utter a warning? The company now asking for a provincial charter in Quebec possesses a boundless appetite. According to official notices in the press it wants to secure not only the area extending from Mont Laurier to Senneterre but also the tract from St. Remi d'Amherst to Mont Laurier and thence to the Great Lake-Chibougamau district. Obviously, therefore, the economic prosperity of our province and the successful operation of our national railway system demand that vigorous steps be taken at once by this government in order to hasten the construction of this line, and also to take over an area that really belongs to the Canadian National Railways, leaving to the Goldfields Transportation Company the privilege of connecting Mont Laurier with Senneterre. I bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) in order to fulfill my responsibility as member for Labelle. Should this government not avail itself of this splendid opportunity of bringing

The Budget-Mr. Lalonde
under its control this area which offers such possibilities from the standpoint of revenue and mining development?
In the second place, may I be permitted to point out to the government the fact that the constituency of Labelle has not been pampered by the federal authorities in the past in regard to the trans-Canada highway from Montreal to Ottawa. I should like to read certain documents, showing that the Quebec government of that time decided upon a change in the route that will be detrimental to my constituency. On May 15, 1936, I placed a question on the order paper, as follows:
1.	What is the location of the proposed trans-Canada highway from Lachute, county of Argenteuil, Quebec, to Ottawa?
2.	Has the location been decided by the provincial or by the federal authorities?
3. Does the highway pass or will it pass through the villages of Fassett, Montebello, Papineauville, Plaisance and Thurso, in the county of Labelle, Quebec?
The reply was:
1,	2 and 3. The route of the trans-Canada highway in the province of Quebec is covered by a report of the Honourable the Executive Council of Quebec, dated October 1, 1931, approved by the lieutenant-governor on October 2, 1931; subsequently amended by a report of the Honourable the Executive Council of Quebec dated March 24, 1933, and approved by the lieutenant-governor on March 25, 1933, and further amended by a report of the Honourable the Executive Council of Quebec dated June 7, 1933, approved by the lieutenant-governor on June 8, 1933, copies of which executive orders are attached hereto.
Copies of these reports in French were attached, and with the permission of the house I will place them on Hansard:
Copy of the Report of a Committee of the Honourable the Executive Council, dated the 1st of October, 1931, approved by the Lieutenant-Governor on the 2nd of October, 1931.
Respecting the Trans-Canada Highway
The Honourable the Minister of Roads, in a memorandum dated the 1st October (1931), recommends:
That a highway running across the province of Quebec be created and designated under the name of the Trans-Canada Highway.
That such highway be constituted as follows: Highway No. 2, from the New Brunswick limit between Saint-Jacques, New Brunswick, and Sainte-Rose-du-Degele, province of Quebec, as far as the city of Levis, passing through the town of Riviere du Loup, and following the riverside road between the village of Andre-ville and Sainte-Anne de la Pocatiere.
Highway No. 3. starting from the city of Levis as far as the intersection of Highway No. 1.
Highway No. 1, passing by the Quebec bridge, from the intersection of Highway No. 3, as far as Quebec.
Highway No. 2, starting from Quebec as far as Montreal, following the riverside road between Saint-Sulpice and Charlemangne.
Highway No. 8, from Montreal to Hull.
Certified.
(Signed) A. Morisset,
Clerk Executive Council.
Copy of the Report of a Committee of the Honourable the Executive Council, dated March 24, 1933, approved by the Lieutenant-Governor on March 25, 1933.
Respecting the Trans-Canada Highway, in the Province of Quebec
The Honourable the Minister of Roads, in a memorandum dated March 24 (1933), recommends that order in council No. 2510, approved on October 2, 1931, respecting the location of the Trans-Canada Highway, in the province of Quebec, be amended so that the location of that transcontinental highway, between Montreal and Ottawa, follows highway No. 8, as far as Grenville, at which point it would pass over the interprovincial bridge on the Ottawa river, and thence toward the dominion capital, on the Ontario side.
Certified.
(Signed) A. Morisset,
Clerk Executive Council.
This ought to be sufficient, Mr. Speaker, to prove that for no reason at all we have been robbed of our share of the trans-Canada highway. In January of this year I had the following question placed on the order paper:
1.	Since July 1, 1936, has the government of the province of Quebec recommended to the dominion government that the location of the trans-Canada highway from Montreal to Ottawa be changed to serve the actual line of highway No. 8 from Grenville to Hull?
2.	If so, what is the date of the recommendation?
Answer: No.
By the end of January last I had communicated with the provincial authorities of Quebec, without receiving any reply. The municipalities concerned, Fassett, Montebello, Papineauville, Plaisance and Thurso, have passed resolutions requesting that the highway follow its former route, but this has not brought about any practical result.
I make this statement, Mr. Speaker, not with a view to criticizing the government of Quebec but so that the people in my constituency may know the facts of the matter, and for that reason only. In making this statement I suggest to all those interested in the welfare of the provincial constituency of Papineau that they should cooperate and exert their influence and authority in order that we from Labelle may also have a few crumbs from the rich man's table, that we may recover what has been taken away from us, and that our unemployed may be given a little work and bread.
Whiat can we infer from the two foregoing suggestions? I respectfully submit, that by

cooperation between tie dominion and provincial governments we should undertake without delay the works I have mentioned, which would prove a real gold mine for the indigent of the western part of the province of Quebec. It is true that tlus year unemployment has been almost unknown ini the northern section of my riding, but it has been very acute in the southern portion of the federal constituency of Labelle. With the construction of the railway referred1 to, and the trans-Canada highway going through the provincial county of Papineau, we would be in a position very materially to assist the unemployed who, tired of begging and of finding themselves under the dire necessity of looking to the state for their living, would find a noble pride in providing for their families by the sweat of their brow.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) of the loyalty and' sincere desire of the electors of Labelle to cooperate. In return I trust that he will let us have access to the treasury, not with a view to making a wholesale distribution of direct relief, which is most depressing, but in order to make ample and generous allotment of the moneys that are paid to the state by way of taxation. Such a gesture, by the magic of the work done by our Canadians, would produce an active and profitable asset.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is a pleasure for me to address the house in English for the first time, as I wish to prove to the extremists as well as the slackers that the prosperity of Canada, if dependent upon economic factors, imponderables and mysteries, lies mainly in the true union and efficient cooperation of the two great races which, having equal rights, live and constitute Canadian life, and which create and defend the ideals of their homeland.
